questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'End of the Congress System' refers to.
questions.a: The Congress system refers to the long period after independence in which the Indian National Congress dominated national politics as a broad umbrella party; its decline began in the late 1960s and accelerated after the 1989 elections, ending the era of one-party dominance at the Centre.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'End of the Congress System'.
questions.a: The Congress party's decline was caused by internal splits, the rise of regional and caste-based parties, the Emergency of 1975-77, and growing electoral competition, which ended its position as the natural party of government.

questions.q: Under which section is 'End of the Congress System' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Era of One-Party Dominance and its Decline

concepts.title: Rise of the BJP and Hindutva Politics

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Rise of the BJP and Hindutva Politics' refers to.
questions.a: The rise of the BJP refers to the growth of the Bharatiya Janata Party from the late 1980s as a major national party advocating Hindutva, cultural nationalism, and a distinct alternative to the Congress-led secular consensus.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Rise of the BJP and Hindutva Politics'.
questions.a: The BJP's rise was driven by the Ayodhya movement, the decline of Congress, the mobilisation of Hindu nationalist sentiment, and the formation of coalition alliances that expanded its electoral reach.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Rise of the BJP and Hindutva Politics' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Rise of New Political Forces

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'The Coalition Era' refers to.
questions.a: The coalition era refers to the period from 1989 to 2014 in which no single party won a majority in the Lok Sabha and national governments were formed through coalitions of multiple parties, often led by a large party with regional allies.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'The Coalition Era'.
questions.a: The coalition era reflected the fragmentation of the party system, the growing importance of regional parties, and the need for consensus-based governance at the Centre.

questions.q: Under which section is 'The Coalition Era' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Coalition Politics

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Mandal Commission and OBC Politics' refers to.
questions.a: The Mandal Commission was set up in 1979 under B.P. Mandal to identify the socially and educationally backward classes and recommend reservations; its implementation in 1990 reserved 27 percent of central government jobs for Other Backward Classes (OBCs).

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Mandal Commission and OBC Politics'.
questions.a: The implementation of the Mandal recommendations politicised caste identity, expanded the OBC vote bank, and strengthened caste-based parties, deeply reshaping Indian electoral politics.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Mandal Commission and OBC Politics' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Caste and Social Justice

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Economic Reforms of 1991' refers to.
questions.a: The economic reforms of 1991 were a package of liberalisation, privatisation, and globalisation measures introduced by the Narasimha Rao government to overcome a severe balance of payments crisis and restructure the Indian economy.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Economic Reforms of 1991'.
questions.a: The 1991 reforms dismantled the licence-permit-quota raj, opened the economy to private investment and foreign trade, and integrated India more closely with the global economy.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Economic Reforms of 1991' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: New Economic Policy

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Ayodhya and Communal Politics' refers to.
questions.a: Ayodhya and communal politics refer to the political mobilisation around the disputed Ram Janmabhoomi-Babri Masjid site at Ayodhya, which became a symbol of Hindu-Muslim tension and a major issue in Indian electoral politics from the late 1980s.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Ayodhya and Communal Politics'.
questions.a: The Ayodhya issue deepened communal polarisation, linked religious identity to electoral competition, and raised serious concerns about the secular character of Indian politics.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Ayodhya and Communal Politics' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Communalism and Identity

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Coalition Governments: NDA and UPA' refers to.
questions.a: The NDA (National Democratic Alliance) led by the BJP and the UPA (United Progressive Alliance) led by the Congress were the two major coalition formations that governed India during the coalition era, reflecting a multi-party system at the national level.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Coalition Governments: NDA and UPA'.
questions.a: The NDA and UPA represented the institutionalisation of coalition politics, in which a large national party led a front of regional and ideological allies to form stable central governments.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Coalition Governments: NDA and UPA' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Coalition Experiments

concepts.title: India in the New World Order

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'India in the New World Order' refers to.
questions.a: India in the new world order refers to the reorientation of Indian foreign policy after the end of the Cold War and the disintegration of the USSR, as India adapted to a unipolar world, economic globalisation, and new strategic partnerships.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'India in the New World Order'.
questions.a: After the Cold War India moved from non-alignment to a multi-directional foreign policy, deepened economic engagement with the global economy, and built new strategic relationships with the United States, Russia, and other powers.

questions.q: Under which section is 'India in the New World Order' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Foreign Policy after the Cold War

concepts.title: Consolidation of Democracy and Contemporary Challenges

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Consolidation of Democracy and Contemporary Challenges' refers to.
questions.a: The consolidation of democracy refers to the deepening and stabilisation of democratic institutions and practices in India despite the challenges of communalism, caste politics, economic inequality, and regional conflicts in the post-1989 period.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Consolidation of Democracy and Contemporary Challenges'.
questions.a: Recent developments show that Indian democracy has become more inclusive and participatory through coalition politics, decentralisation, and social justice, even as it faces persistent challenges of communal polarisation and inequality.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Consolidation of Democracy and Contemporary Challenges' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Assessment of Recent Developments
